README.md
content:
# Shiny App

This folder contains the modular Shiny application:

- `global.R` loads data and shared configuration;
- `ui.R` defines the interface; and
- `server.R` implements filtering, criterion relationships, and reports.

The app reads its source files from `data/`.

From the repository root, run:

```r
shiny::runApp("app")
```

From this `app` directory, run:

```r
shiny::runApp(".")
```

Run the full lookup-table validator from the repository root before publishing
data changes:

```r
source("validate_app_data.R")
```

See the [project README](../README.md) for package requirements, filtering
logic, criteria relationships, data schemas, and report behavior.

"1","Prediction","Foundational","General","Species-environment equilibrium","SDMs often assume that a species is in equilibrium (or quasi-equilibrium) with the environment in which it occurs. That is, suitable habitat is fully occupied or saturated (e.g., Gallien et al. 2012, Zurell et al. 2024).","This assumption can be violated in several ways. For instance, the species range can be restricted by biotic interactions (e.g., competition, predation, pathogens, disturbances; Richmond et al. 2010), leaving portions of their suitable habitat unoccupied. In addition, for invasive species, the extent to which the invader occupies their suitable environment varies depending on the stage of invasion (Gallien et al. 2012). Dispersal barriers may also prevent invader and range-shifting species from reaching suitable habitats (Foster et al. 2022, Marjakangas et al. 2023; see criteria “No dispersal limitation”). There is also increasing evidence that range-shifting species are lagging behind their climatically suitable habitat (Svenning et al. 2008), leading to suitable habitat with delayed colonization (“colonisation credit”) and delayed extinction (“extinction debt”; Foden et al 2007, Foster et al. 2022, Zurell et al. 2024). Additionally, the chances of violating this criteria increase with the extent of the study region (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024).","Use historical range information for model training., Develop a dispersal model to best estimate the species potential distribution (Merow et al. 2016)., Include species' ecological traits in SDMs (Hanspach et al. 2010; Jiguet et al. 2010; Viana & Chase 2022)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption., Can we use disequilibrium indicators (e.g. filled vs. unfilled regional niches) to predict a species' future spread or adaptation potential?., ""Use models that incorporate biological processes (e.g. thermal limits, energetics) rather than just statistical correlations, as these better capture real-world limitations beyond simple climate."", ""Add functions relating occurrence likelihood to distance from known locations to account for dispersal limitations and mass effects, improving niche models."", Implement Nested SDMs (N-SDMs; Guisan et al. 2025).","If a model assumes that suitable habitat is fully occupied when in fact it is not, it is well understood that the model may underestimate suitable habitat in areas with missing species presences in the model training step (Welk 2004, Richmond et al. 2010, Václavík & Meentemeyer 2012). Evidence also exists for overestimated suitable habitat in areas not occupied by the species (e.g., due to competition and dispersal limitation; Lowen et al. 2019).","Always","Always","3, 4.2, 33","6","3, 4.2, 33, 6","Gallien et al. 2012; Zurell et al. 2024; Richmond et al. 2010; Foster et al. 2022; Marjakangas et al. 2023; Svenning et al. 2008; Foden et al. 2007; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Merow et al. 2016; Hanspach et al. 2010; Jiguet et al. 2010; Viana & Chase 2022; Guisan et al. 2025; Welk 2004; Václavík & Meentemeyer 2012; Lowen et al. 2019"
"1","Projection","Foundational","General","Species-environment equilibrium","SDMs often assume that a species is in equilibrium (or quasi-equilibrium) with the environment in which it occurs. That is, suitable habitat is fully occupied or saturated (e.g., Gallien et al. 2012, Zurell et al. 2024).","This assumption can be violated in several ways. For instance, the species range can be restricted by biotic interactions (e.g., competition, predation, pathogens, disturbances; Richmond et al. 2010), leaving portions of their suitable habitat unoccupied. Evidence also exists for overestimated suitable habitat in areas not occupied by the species (e.g., due to “colonization credit”; e.g., Zurell et al. 2024, Haddou et al. 2022).","Always","Always","3, 4.2","6","3, 4.2, 6","Gallien et al. 2012; Zurell et al. 2024; Richmond et al. 2010; Foster et al. 2022; Marjakangas et al. 2023; Svenning et al. 2008; Foden et al. 2007; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Merow et al. 2016; Hanspach et al. 2010; Jiguet et al. 2010; Viana & Chase 2022; Guisan et al. 2025; Welk 2004; Václavík & Meentemeyer 2012; Haddou et al. 2022"
"2","Prediction","Foundational","General","Niche stability","SDMs typically assume that species maintain their ecological niche (the set of environmental conditions they require to thrive) across space and time. That is, ""the notion that the niche envelope is a fixed and immutable characteristic of a species, unchanging over space and time"" (Wiens et al. 2009).","This assumption can be violated in several ways. For example, invasive species may develop adaptations to local conditions (biotic or abiotic) and thus occupy areas outside their native environmental niche (Gallien et al. 2012, Gallien et al. 2010, Weins et al. 2009). Ongoing and future climate change may also lead to rapid evolutionary (particularly in the case of short-generation species; Wiens et al. 2009, Franks et al. 2007) or behavioural adaptations to environmental conditions (e.g., changes in timing of spring migration or breeding activity in birds; Root et al. 2003). The probability of violation also depends on the speed of change, the forecasting horizon (i.e., long-term forecasts are more susceptible as greater evolutionary and/or behaviour change may accumulate), and the spatial extent of the analysis (the larger the extent, the greater the likelihood of non-stationarity; Pease et al. 2022).","Shorten timescale of analysis., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","For prediction models, under and overestimation can occur, but are dependent on sampling and ecological context (Bryn et al. 2021). "4.1","Prediction","Foundational","General","Eltonian noise (positive interactions)","The Eltonian noise hypothesis states that local biotic interactions do not alter species’ environmental niches at larger scales, only introduce statistical noise. Instead, species niche is assumed to be dominantly determined by climate (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Most SDMs rely on this hypothesis and thus, often only include abiotic variables as predictors. Yet, biotic interactions are among the reasons why a species may not be at equilibrium with their environment (Richmond et al. 2010, Jeschke & Strayer 2008).","There is growing evidence that this assumption can be frequently violated, supported by improved SDMs when biotic interactions are included (e.g., Fern et al. 2019, Boulangeat et al. 2012, Godsoe & Harmon 2012, Suttle et al. 2007). In some cases (e.g., boreal caribou, wolf, and moose; Boutin et al. 2012), there is evidence that competition and/or predation restrict the distribution of species (Poggiato et al. 2025). In other cases, it is clear that mutualism and/or symbiosis allow species to persist. By ignoring biotic interactions, SDMs may capture the Grinnellian (fundamental bioclimatic) niche instead of the Eltonian (realized biotic) niche (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). However, Godsoe & Harmon (2012) highlight that violation of this assumption is not universal. Instead, it depends on the species, type of biotic interaction, and modelling method (Araújo & Luoto 2007). "13","Prediction","Data quality, relevance and preparation","Species datasets","Independence of species observations","Much like most statistical methods, SDMs rely on the assumption of independence of observations, that is, that each recorded species presence (or absence) is a unique sample, not influenced by or correlated to nearby records (i.e., not spatially autocorrelated; Guisan & Thuiller 2005).","This assumption can be easily and frequently violated in ecology. Even if surveys are systematically designed to cover the study extent uniformly and randomly, the species distribution itself is not random (Guisan et al. 2017). Beyond the underlying habitat preferences, a number of ecological and behavioural (intrinsic) factors can result in spatial autocorrelation in species occurrences (or absences), including reproduction, site fidelity, dispersal limitation, home range size, territoriality, and more (Paradinas et al. 2023, Wintle & Bardos 2006). Therefore, surveys may detect the same individual multiple times or multiple individuals of the same population in the same or nearby locations. Alternatively, if intraspecific competition is strong, the detection of one individual at a location may decrease the likelihood of detecting another. Extrinsic factors such as spatially structured environmental processes and patterns, can also lead to spatial autocorrelation in species distribution and therefore lead to violation (Dormann et al. 2007, Wintle & Bardos 2006).","Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","An SDM aims to explain a species’ pattern of spatial distribution by means of environmental predictors. If the model is successful, no spatial autocorrelation should be left in the model residuals (Guisan et al. 2017). Instead, when the model residuals are spatially autocorrelated, it indicates that intrinsic and/or extrinsic factors were not covered by the model. The main consequence of this violation is an increase in Type I error (false positive) when identifying predictors (Paradinas et al. 2023, Dormann et al. 2007). In terms of prediction error, overestimation of suitable habitat is more likely to occur (e.g., through an inflated estimate of habitat preference; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). But, if important predictors are missing, it can also lead to underestimation of suitable habitat (e.g., through niche truncation; Guisan et al. 2025). This applies to both prediction and projection models, but projection models may suffer further due to the additional temporal and spatio-temporal autocorrelation (Dormann et al. 2007).","Sometimes","Always","","","","Guisan & Thuiller 2005; Guisan et al. 2017; Paradinas et al. 2023; Wintle & Bardos 2006; Dormann et al. 2007; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Guisan et al. 2025"

"16.1","Prediction","Data quality, relevance and preparation","Predictors datasets","Predictors resolution matches response scale (spatial)","The spatial resolution of predictors should match the resolution at which the response variable is affected by the predictors (Araújo et al. 2019, Wiens et al. 2009). ","This criteria is violated by mismatches in spatial scales between the species responses and the predictor variables. "19","Prediction","Data quality, relevance and preparation","Predictors datasets","Uncertainty in predictor variables is accounted for","Uncertainty in predictor variables is an inherent factor of SDMs (McInerny & Purves 2011). Since it is essentially impossible to guarantee zero errors in mapped environmental predictors – which can be introduced in a variety of ways, including instrument measurement error, spatial scaling, geo-registration, interpolation (Araújo et al. 2019, McInerny & Purves 2011, Barry & Elith 2006) – SDMs should include quantification of sources of uncertainty. Ideally, modellers should quantify the effects of the relevant predictor uncertainties on SDM outputs; at a minimum, likely sources of uncertainty should be acknowledged and their possible effects on SDM results discussed (Araújo et al. 2019). Additionally, when using model products with inherent uncertainties (e.g., climate change models), those should also be accounted for (Cheaib et al. 2012).","This criteria is violated when modellers use predictor variables with no consideration of errors and uncertainty (Araújo et al. 2019).","Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","When uncertainties in predictor variables are unaccounted for, they can lead to bias in the estimates of the model's parameters. Specifically, when violation leads to a predictor variable that fails to capture fine-scale variation (i.e., attenuation bias) and the species is known to respond to particular conditions (e.g., a strict physiological temperature constraint), both underestimation and overestimation of suitable habitat is reported to occur in prediction and projection models owing to a flattened response curve (Stoklosa et al. 2015, McInerny & Purves 2011). In the same way that an overly smooth predictor layer can miss identifying specialized habitat requirements, thus leading to underestimation, it can also incorrectly associate species presences to other more widespread conditions, leading to overestimation. Violation can also lead to a loss of power (i.e., ability to determine which predictor variables are most important; Stoklosa et al. 2015) when there are strong spatial patterns in predictor variable errors. As the relationships between variables may change across space and/or time, this can also lead to prediction errors (Barry and Elith 2006). While ignoring predictor uncertainty introduces attenuation bias, the severity of its effect are likely to be weakened in the following cases: for prediction models where the uncertainty is systematic and uniform across the study area (Barry and Elith 2006); for generalist species with wide tolerances (Velásquez-Tibatá et al. 2016); when modeling biodiversity trends at ecoregional or continental scales (Seo et al. 2008).","Sometimes","Sometimes","","","","McInerny & Purves 2011; Araújo et al. 2019; Barry & Elith 2006; Cheaib et al. 2012; Stoklosa et al. 2015; Velásquez-Tibatá et al. 2016; Seo et al. 2008"

"21.2","Prediction","Model building","Model settings/complexity","Model complexity and structure are appropriate (over fit models)","The Eltonian noise hypothesis states that local biotic interactions do not alter species’ environmental niches at larger scales, only introduce statistical noise. Instead, species niche is assumed to be dominantly determined by climate (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Most SDMs rely on this hypothesis and thus, often only include abiotic variables as predictors. Yet, biotic interactions are among the reasons why a species may not be at equilibrium with their environment (Richmond et al. 2010, Jeschke & Strayer 2008).","There is growing evidence that this assumption can be frequently violated, supported by improved SDMs when biotic interactions are included (e.g., Fern et al. 2019, Boulangeat et al. 2012, Godsoe & Harmon 2012, Suttle et al. 2007). In some cases (e.g., boreal caribou, wolf, and moose; Boutin et al. 2012), there is evidence that competition and/or predation restrict the distribution of species (Poggiato et al. 2025). In other cases, it is clear that mutualism and/or symbiosis allow species to persist. By ignoring biotic interactions, SDMs may capture the Grinnellian (fundamental bioclimatic) niche instead of the Eltonian (realized biotic) niche (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). However, Godsoe & Harmon (2012) highlight that violation of this assumption is not universal. Instead, it depends on the species, type of biotic interaction, and modelling method (Araújo & Luoto 2007). Additionally, the chances of violating this criteria increase with the extent of the study region (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024).","Comparing a range of models (predictive performance) & response shapes (Ramampiandra et al. 2023)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","‘Over fit’ prediction models often lead to underestimation of suitable habitat by ascribing pattern to noise and resulting in highly specific species-environmental relationships (Merow et al. 2014).","Always","Rarely","12, 26, 27, 29, 33","","12, 26, 27, 29, 33","Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Richmond et al. 2010; Jeschke & Strayer 2008; Fern et al. 2019; Boulangeat et al. 2012; Godsoe & Harmon 2012; Suttle et al. 2007; Boutin et al. 2012; Poggiato et al. 2025; Araújo & Luoto 2007; Ramampiandra et al. 2023; Merow et al. 2014"

"30","Prediction","Model assessment","Model estimates","Performance/evaluation metrics are appropriate","The performance of a model can be assessed in many different ways. Araújo et al. (2019) suggests three dimensions of evaluation: realism, accuracy, and generality. Which dimension(s) to evaluate will depend on the question and model objective but typically, evaluation metrics (i.e., statistical tools used to evaluate model outputs) are concerned with model accuracy and generality. In turn, defining which model performance metrics are appropriate and exhaustively summarize model performance depends primarily on the structure of the species occurrence data (i.e., presence-absence or presence-only) and on the type of the response variable (e.g., count, presence-absence; Guisan et al. 2017). Other factors such as the robustness of the metric to species prevalence (i.e., the proportion of sampled sites where the species is present versus absent) or the requirement for a threshold-dependent versus -independent metric given the research objective should also be taken into account. For guidance on selecting appropriate metrics, see Guisan et al. (2017).","This criteria can be violated in multiple ways. For example, a projection model violates this criteria if it fails to evaluate its generality (Araújo et al. 2019). A model built using presence-only and pseudo-absence data violates this criteria if computing statistics such as AUC (area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve) and TSS (true skill statistic) that require the use of true absences to calculate the confusion matrix (Guillaumot et al. 2019). Jiménez-Valverde (2012) also suggests that “[w]hen the potential distribution is the goal of the research, the AUC is not an appropriate performance measure because the weight of commission errors is much lower than that of omission errors”.","Selecting the Right Metrics: Different metrics (AUC, TSS, Kappa, Tjur's R2), etc.) evaluate different aspects of model performance (e.g. discrimination, calibration, accuracy) and respond differently to factors like species prevalence., ""Consider Ecological Plausibility: Do not just focus on a high performance score; ensure that the model's relationships with environmental variables are ecologically relevant and make sense based on existing knowledge of the species (e.g. expected temperature responses)."", Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","When model assessment fails to employ the appropriate evaluation metrics, it risks not capturing or inappropriately assessing prediction errors and other potential shortcomings in the model performance. In other words, the incorrect metric will not cause a prediction error, but it can compromise the ability to correctly detect prediction error. For example, when modelling rare species, inappropriate metrics may inflate the sense of accuracy and miss the detection of underestimation or overestimation (Allouche et al. 2006). Alternatively, in the case of modelling potential distribution, an evaluation metric that weights false negatives and false positives equally will be misleading, as overestimation is unlikely a concern (Jiménez-Valverde 2012). "12","Prediction","Data quality, relevance and preparation","Species datasets","Species data sample size is appropriate","Sample size is a major limiting factor of SDMs (Thibaud et al. 2014). SDMs assume that the effective sample size of species occurrences is appropriate for the statistical analysis, as accuracy should increase until it asymptotes with increasing sample sizes (Hernandez et al. 2006). The appropriate sample size, however, depends on a number of factors, including the species’ range size and niche width, spatial resolution, number of predictor variables, the complexity of the species-environment relationships, and modelling method (Moudrý et al. 2024, Santini et al. 2021, Stockwell & Peterson 2002).","This criteria can be frequently violated when modelling rare species, cryptic species, or those difficult to detect for other reasons (e.g., observable only during brief time windows; Radomski et al. 2022). Fulfilling this criteria may also be impracticable for species that have restricted geographic ranges (Santini et al. 2021). Other limitations on data availability can also lead to violation. Lastly, even generally accepted minimal sample sizes can commonly lead to violation as they reflect requirements under optimal conditions (e.g., niche stability, no dispersal limitation, no spatial position error, etc.; Moudrý et al. 2024).","It requires careful consideration of the purpose of the study (Moudrý et al. 2024)., Consider species' ecology: SDMs better predict specialist species with narrow ecological niches than generalist species with wider ecological niches (Tsoar et al. 2007) (Moudrý et al. 2024)., Consider the number of predictors investigated. As the ability to differentiate between influential and non-influential variables decreases with decreasing sample sizes (Moudrý et al. 2024)., Consider the complexity of the shape of species response curves must be taken into account as models based on small sample sizes result in less precise estimates of these shapes (Bazzichetto et al. 2023) (Moudrý et al. 2024)., Consider testing the effect of sample size (Moudrý et al. 2024; see also van van Proosdij et al. 2016)., Consider designing accurate SDMs with a well-balanced sampling of as few as 50 presences (Moudrý et al. 2024)., Subsampling; weighting; inputation (see Bowler et al. 2025)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","As Hernandez et al. (2006) point out, “[s]mall sample sizes pose challenges to any statistical analyses and result in decreased predictive potential when compared to models developed with more occurrences”. This can express itself in a few different ways. When a small sample size leads to environmental sampling bias, its consequences can be explained by violations of the criteria “Species data covers the environmental extent” (Hernandez et al. 2006). A limited sample size also constrains model complexity, that is, the model’s capacity to capture the underlying species-environmental relationships (Moudrý et al. 2024). In this case, consequences can be explained by violations of the criteria “Model complexity and structure are appropriate”.","","10, 21.1, 21.2","","10, 21.1, 21.2","12 > 10; 12 > 21.1; 12 > 21.2","Thibaud et al. 2014; Hernandez et al. 2006; Moudrý et al. 2024; Santini et al. 2021; Stockwell & Peterson 2002; Radomski et al. 2022; Tsoar et al. 2007; Bazzichetto et al. 2023; van Proosdij et al. 2016; Bowler et al. 2025"
"26","Prediction","Model building","Model settings/complexity","Statistical methods and algorithms employed are appropriate","Several algorithms and approaches are now available for building SDMs. However, the appropriate choices depend primarily on the available species occurrence data and the model objective (Wiens et al. 2009, Elith & Leathwick 2009). For instance, count data require specifying an appropriate probability distribution function (e.g., Poisson, negative binomial) and an algorithm that supports it, such as generalized regressions or boosted regression trees (Guisan et al. 2017). Some methods require binary response variables (i.e., species presence-absence, or pseudoabsence), including generalized linear models (GLMs) or generalized additive models (GAMs; Wiens et al. 2009). Additionally, binary data require binomial probability distribution functions and logistic transformation (Guisan et al. 2017). Regarding the model objective, different statistical approaches are preferred when the goal is explanation, prediction and projection (Guisan et al. 2017, Elith & Leathwick 2009); although, the literature suggests that for any particular goal, there is no “best” overall model (Lawler et al. 2006).","This criteria can be easily violated when modelers use default settings in model parametrization without confirming whether they are appropriate choices for their species occurrence data (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Similarly, violation can occur through the use of an algorithm that is inappropriate for the data type or whose underlying mathematical distribution does not match the data type.","Consider ensemble models., Assess model performance; using Tru Skill Statistics (e.g. Shabani et al. 2016; Allouche et al. 2006)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption. Evaluate a set of candidate models using independent data (if available) or robust cross-validation methods to assess their fit and predictive power., Manage model complexity: Overly complex models with many parameters can overfit the data and perform poorly when extrapolating to new conditions. Balance complexity with data availability to ensure reliable predictions.","Violation of this criteria can lead to errors and uncertainty in the predictions by introducing structural biases and statistical distortions. In terms of prediction errors, consequences can be explained by violation of the related criteria “Model complexity and structure are appropriate”.","","21.1, 21.2","","21.1, 21.2","26 > 21.1; 26 > 21.2","Wiens et al. 2009; Elith & Leathwick 2009; Guisan et al. 2017; Lawler et al. 2006; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Shabani et al. 2016; Allouche et al. 2006"
"27","Prediction","Model building","Model settings/complexity","Shape of the species and predictors relationships is appropriate","Related to the criteria “Model complexity and structure are appropriate”, SDMs rely on fitting a correlative relationship between the species occurrence data and predictor variables. Species responses to environmental factors are often non-linear (e.g., a bell-shaped curve describing optimal thermal tolerances, rather than a straight line; Austin 2002). Goodness-of-fit depends on properly describing the species-environmental relationships while balancing model complexity (Merow et al. 2014, Guisan et al. 2017).","This criteria is violated when modellers mischaracterize relationships between species and predictor variables (e.g., by using modelling approaches that do not handle non-linear relationships).","Transform covariates., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","When this criteria is violated, its consequences can be explained by violation of the criteria ""Model complexity and structure are appropriate"".","","21.1, 21.2","","21.1, 21.2","27 > 21.1; 27 > 21.2","Austin 2002; Merow et al. 2014; Guisan et al. 2017"
"28","Prediction","Model building","Model settings/complexity","Background points or pseduo-absences are appropriate","Most SDM approaches rely on presence-only data combined with background points or pseudo-absences (Steen et al. 2024, Barbet-Massin et al. 2012). Background points correspond to points across the study area that are used to characterize the predictor variables at each site, regardless of whether species occurrence has been sampled at those points and whether the species has been detected (Araújo et al. 2019). Although the term is often used interchangeably with pseudo-absences, these correspond to sites chosen to represent absences, regardless of confirmation of true absences (Liu et al. 2019; also see Senay et al. 2013). Although many approaches exist for selecting background points and pseudo-absence points, the accuracy of SDMs depends on choosing the appropriate method given the modelling context (Steen et al. 2024, Senay et al. 2013, Barbet-Massin et al. 2012).","This criteria is violated in three main ways: if the background points are not representative of the available environment space to appropriately describe the species niche (Steen et al. 2024, Barbet-Massin et al. 2012); similarly, if pseudo-absences are either restricted to an overly tight geographic buffer around known presences or taken from an overly broad area (Barbet-Massin et al. 2012); and if the criteria “Unbiased species data” and “Biases and noise in species datasets are treated” have been violated (e.g., randomly selecting background points and/or pseudo-absences when presence data is highly biased/clustered; Phillips et al. 2009).","Assess predcitive performance; using different types of background selections (Steen et al. 2024)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","When this criteria is violated by background points that are not representative of the species environment space, its consequences can be explained by violation of the criteria “Species data covers the environmental extent”. If this criteria is violated through violation of the criteria “Biases and noise in species datasets are treated”, see criteria “Unbiased species data” for consequences. When violation happens due to pseudo-absences that are overly close to presence points, thus likely corresponding to suitable habitat, models are known to underestimate suitable habitat (Chefaoui & Lobo 2008). In contrast, when pseudo-absences are taken from an overly broad area that captures different environmental conditions than those experienced by the species, models suffer from an artificially inflated sense of confidence. By failing to learn to distinguish subtle environmental requirements, the model results in overestimation of suitable habitat (Barbet-Massin et al. 2012). These cases of prediction error apply to both prediction and projection models.","","10","10","10","28 > 10; 28 > 9 > 10","Steen et al. 2024; Barbet-Massin et al. 2012; Araújo et al. 2019; Liu et al. 2019; Senay et al. 2013; Phillips et al. 2009; Chefaoui & Lobo 2008"
"29","Prediction","Model building","Reducing predictors","Predictor variables are appropriately reduced, if applicable","Predictor variable reduction is a common approach for treating collinearity and reducing model complexity to minimize overfitting (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). However, steps should be taken to ensure that variable reduction is done without compromising the model’s ability to fit nuances if informative data are discarded (even if variables might be collinear; Dormann et al. 2013), thus reducing the predictive ability of the model (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024).","This criteria is violated when modellers apply variable reduction methods without considering the ecological relevance of variables (e.g., through pre-determined cutoffs in correlation analyses; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Araújo et al. 2019).","Assess spatial autocorrelation in model residuals., Use spatial autoregressive models., Use spatial eigenvector mapping., Remove collinear variables to reduce redundancy., Reduce dimenssiionality (Zhang et al. 2023)., Orthogonal Principal Componenents (Farrell et al. 2019)., Algorithms might account for redundant variables (e.g.; Feng et al. 2019)., Select environmental variables for groups of species with similar natural histories (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024) ., Variable selection approach (Cobos et al. 2019)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","Violation of this criteria leads to violation of the related criteria “Model complexity and structure are appropriate”.","","21.1, 21.2","","21.1, 21.2","29 > 21.1; 29 > 21.2","Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Dormann et al. 2013; Araújo et al. 2019; Zhang et al. 2023; Farrell et al. 2019; Feng et al. 2019; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Cobos et al. 2019"
"32","Prediction","Model assessment","Validation","Model training and validation datasets are appropriate","As Araújo et al. (2019) point out, “[a] key step in evaluating models is to compare their results against statistically independent data”. The golden standard is to use species occurrence data that are spatially or temporally independent from the training data (i.e., from separate geographic areas or data collected in different time periods; e.g., Finn et al. 2024, Hintze et al. 2021). When fully independent data is not available, training and validation datasets can be created by subsetting the data following an appropriate data partitioning method given the data structure and model objective (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Araújo et al. 2019, Le Rest et al. 2014, Araújo et al. 2005). For prediction models, although less ideal, evaluation can be also done by sub-sampling the training data when the sample size is small (e.g., Hijmans et al. 2012).","When independent data is not available, this criteria can be easily violated when creating training and validation sets since most observations are related to each other in a spatial context (Le Rest et al. 2014). In this case, the main way violation can occur is by employing data partitioning methods that rely on random splits of the data; despite being a well supported collection of methods (e.g., k-fold partitioning, bootstrapping, jack-knifing), random splits of occurrence data do not ensure statistical independence or treat biases, and therefore are still sensitive to spatial and/or temporal autocorrelation in the data (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Araújo et al. 2005).","Splitting data non-randomly (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","Violation of this criteria will compromise the ability of the validation step to detect a model that fits biased and/or autocorrelated training data (e.g., Fourcade et al. 2018, Hijmans et al. 2012; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Therefore, its consequences can be explained by violation of the criteria “Unbiased species data” and “Biases and noise in species datasets are treated”.","","","10","10","32 > 9 > 10; 32 > 22 > 9 > 10","Araújo et al. 2019; Finn et al. 2024; Hintze et al. 2021; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Rest et al. 2014; Araújo et al. 2005; Hijmans et al. 2012; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Fourcade et al. 2018"
"33","Prediction","Model assessment","Extrapolation","Extrapolation approach is appropriate","Projection models often require making predictions into new, non-analog conditions (i.e., not present in the training data and/or region; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Beyond quantifying novelty (e.g., Mesgaran et al. 2014) and reporting the uncertainty due to extrapolation (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Zurrel et al. 2020), it is assumed that modelers extrapolate “in a biologically sensible manner” (Zurrel et al. 2020). Deciding between an unconstrained (response continues its trend) or a fixed approach (response is fixed at the last value) can be informed by structural factors, including how different non-analog conditions are from reference, the shape of the response curve at point of truncation, the amount of data available, and model complexity (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Sequeria et al. 2018, Yates et al. 2018). But ultimately, it should reflect biological, ecological, and evolutionary dynamics. Prediction models may also require extrapolation, particularly if other criteria are violated.","The main way this criteria can be violated is through the choice of an inappropriate extrapolation approach. For example, by violating the criteria “Statistical methods and algorithms employed are appropriate”, the modeler might default to using an unconstrained approach when the training model truncates at a species’ thermal tolerance limit, where a fixed approach would be more appropriate (Guevara et al. 2018). Alternatively, if the model only captures a narrow range of tolerances (through violation of the criteria “Species data covers the environmental extent” and/or “Non-novel conditions”) or if the species is known to be highly plastic and adaptive (through violation of the criteria “Genotype and phenotype stability”), violation can happen through defining a fixed approach (Rodríguez et al. 2019). But this criteria can also be violated when other related criteria (“Species-environmental equilibrium”, “Niche stability”, “Model complexity and structure are appropriate”) are violated and the modeller overlooks the effects of extrapolation and/or fails to quantify extrapolation (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Sequeira et al. 2018, Mesgaran et al. 2014).","Assessing suitability curves (Owens et al. 2013)., Identify areas of extrict extrapolation; using index such as MESS and MOP (See Owens et al. 2013)., Flagging areas with high uncertainty due to extrapolation (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024)., Assess model's robustness to extrapolation (e.g.; Roberts et al. 2017)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","Failing to quantify extrapolation may lead to over and/or underestimation. Consequences for prediction models are related to violation of other related criteria (see criteria “Species-environmental equilibrium”, “Niche stability”, and/or “Model complexity and structure are appropriate”).","","1, 2, 21.1, 21.2","","1, 2, 21.1, 21.2","33 > 1; 33 > 2; 33 > 21.1; 33 > 21.2","Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Mesgaran et al. 2014; Zurrel et al. 2020; Sequeria et al. 2018; Yates et al. 2018; Guevara et al. 2018; Rodríguez et al. 2019; Sequeira et al. 2018; Owens et al. 2013; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Roberts et al. 2017"
"22","Prediction","Model building","Treatments, fittings, tunning","Biases and noise in species datasets are treated","When the criteria “Unbiased species data”, “Species data covers the environmental extent”, and/or “Species data covers the geographic extent” are violated (i.e., cannot be corrected), steps should be taken to account for such biases in the model (Araújo et al. 2019). The most supported approach for when access to unbiased data is lacking, is to reduce its effects by choosing background data with the same sampling bias (Vollering et al. 2019, Syfert et al. 2013, Phillips et al. 2009; see Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Other approaches include: accounting for spatial autocorrelation in occurrence data, incorporating a proxy of spatial bias as a covariate, filtering occurrence data to reduce clustering across geographic and/or environmental space, weighting occurrence records so that points in oversampled areas are assigned a smaller weight (Ranc et al. 2017).","This criteria is violated when treatment of bias and noise in species datasets is not appropriate or effective at addressing the issue.","Spatial thining/filtering., Background/Pseudo-absence Point Manipulation approach., Implement Integrated Species Distribution Models (ISDMs) approach that combines data from multiple sources., Applying weights to observations can account for varying sampling reliability or effort., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","When this criteria is violated, its consequences can be explained by violation of its related criteria “Unbiased species data”.","An SDM built on statistical correlations alone and lacking ecological realism may seem robust statistically but lead to misleading results (e.g., Fourcade et al. 2014). The consequences of violation for prediction errors are, however, context dependent. If the model neglects biotic constraints or positive biotic interactions, its consequences are defined by violations to the “Eltonian noise” criteria. If the model neglects anthropogenic and/or geographic constraints, its consequences are defined by violations to the “No dispersal limitation” criteria. If the model fails to account for the ability to adapt to new environments, its consequences are defined by violations to the “Genotype and phenotype stability” criteria. (2019) also emphasize the importance of evenly sampling along the environmental gradients occupied by the taxon within the study area. For the special case of occupancy SDMs, unbiased data should include samples collected from a closed population (i.e., geographically isolated, without immigration and emigration during the sampling period). For example, violation can occur when species occurrence records rely heavily on spatially clumped or incomplete data from museum collections (Richmond et al. 2010). "15","Projection","Data quality, relevance and preparation","Predictors datasets","Predictors spatial resolution matches species data","The spatial resolution of the predictor data should be as close as possible to the spatial accuracy of the occurrence data (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Araújo et al. 2019, Guisan et al. 2007).","There are three main ways in which mismatches between the spatial resolution of the predictor and occurrence data can occur. The first is through spatial positional errors in the occurrence data. Although past consensus suggested that when spatial positional errors are known to occur, the predictor data should be coarser than the largest positional error in the species occurrence data (Gábor et al. 2020, Moudrý & Šímová 2012), new findings indicate that data coarsening can negatively affect SDM performance (Gábor et al. 2022). Instead, if spatial positional errors occur, steps should be taken to correct or minimize them (see criteria “Lack of spatial positional error” for more). The second source of violation is limited data availability at finer resolutions, which in limited cases, can be addressed by downscaling (Araújo et al. 2019, Wiens et al. 2009). Lastly, this criteria can be intentionally violated if a given species-environmental relationship is best modelled at a coarser resolution (e.g., high spatial autocorrelation, climate variables may act at broader spatial scales than biotic interactions or vegetation structure; Gábor et al. 2022).","","For consequences of violation due to spatial positional errors, see criteria “Lack of spatial positional error”. For other cases, the risk of prediction error depends on whether the related criteria “Predictors spatial and temporal resolution matches response scale” is violated. "17","Projection","Data quality, relevance and preparation","Predictors datasets","Predictors are relevant for the species response","While a large number of candidate variables may be available, an SDM should be built using predictors that are known to be causally related to the species response (e.g., distributions, suitable habitat, abundance; Araújo et al. 2019) and niche requirements (Wiens et al. 2009) – also known as proximal or driving factors. Since cause-and-effect relationships are typically difficult to infer, the selection of candidate variables can be statistically supported or defined via testing (e.g., Hong & Cho 2015, Barbosa et al. 2001). Best practices recommend that variables that are only correlated to the species’ distribution (i.e., indirect or proxy variables) should not be used for (explanation and) projection models (Araújo et al. 2019, Wiens et al. 2009).","This criteria can be violated in (explanation and) projection models via the inclusion of proxy variables (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Prediction models built using proxy variables (i.e., correlative prediction SDMs) can also lead to violation if they also violated the criteria “Niche stability”, “Species data covers the environmental extent” and “Species data covers the geographic extent” (Mesgaran et al. 2014).","Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption., ""Modelers might consider this criterion is irrelevant or has minimum impact on the accuracy of model precictions. Modelers are looking only for high model accuracy and low uncertainty, regarless of explaining of predictors.""","For (explanation and) projection models, the inclusion of proxy variables can lead to inaccurate predictions if the correlation between the proxy and driving factors varies across locations and/or time periods (Feng et al. 2019). Therefore, its consequences for prediction error can be explained by violation to the criteria “Niche stability”. Changes in correlation can also occur due to missing driving factors (see criteria “All predictors relevant for the species response are included”; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024).","When geographic sampling biases exist, these can translate into biased species-environment relationships due to niche truncation, and thus violate the criteria “Species data covers the environmental extent ”.","2","","2","17 > 2","Araújo et al. 2019; Wiens et al. 2009; Hong & Cho 2015; Barbosa et al. 2001; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Mesgaran et al. 2014; Feng et al. 2019"
"6","Projection","Foundational","General","Understanding the ecological processes driving species distribution and abundances","SDMs should be built on a strong understanding of the ecological processes driving a species’ distribution, including geographic, biotic and abiotic drivers (Bryn et al. 2021, Elith & Leathwick 2009, Araújo & Guisan 2006). Although automated solutions can be used to aid in predictor selection, it should not eliminate the need to preselect sound predictors based on knowledge of the species (Araújo & Guisan 2006).","This criteria can be easily violated, whether simply due to a shortcoming of the modeler (i.e., lack of knowledge of best practices), or due to true limited availability of complete knowledge on the ecological processes driving a species’ distribution (Bryn et al. 2021).","Include disturbance processes (i.e. fire regimes) as potential predictors of changes in species distributions (e.g.; Vallecillo et al. 2009)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption., ""Modelers might consider this criterion is irrelevant or has minimum impact on the accuracy of model precictions. Modelers are looking only for high model accuracy and low uncertainty, regarless of explaining of predictors.""","An SDM built on statistical correlations alone and lacking ecological realism may seem robust statistically but lead to misleading results (e.g., Fourcade et al. 2014). The consequences of violation for prediction errors are, however, context dependent. If the model neglects biotic constraints or positive biotic interactions, its consequences are defined by violations to the “Eltonian noise” criteria. If the model neglects anthropogenic and/or geographic constraints, its consequences are defined by violations to the “No dispersal limitation” criteria. If the model fails to account for the ability to adapt to new environments, its consequences are defined by violations to the “Genotype and phenotype stability” criteria. Also see criteria “Predictors are relevant for species response” for more information.","","4.1","1","4.1, 1","6 > 4.1; 6 > 4.2 > 1; 6 > 3 > 1","Bryn et al. 2021; Elith & Leathwick 2009; Araújo & Guisan 2006; Vallecillo et al. 2009; Fourcade et al. 2014"
"12","Projection","Data quality, relevance and preparation","Species datasets","Species data sample size is appropriate","Sample size is a major limiting factor of SDMs (Thibaud et al. 2014). SDMs assume that the effective sample size of species occurrences is appropriate for the statistical analysis, as accuracy should increase until it asymptotes with increasing sample sizes (Hernandez et al. 2006). The appropriate sample size, however, depends on a number of factors, including the species’ range size and niche width, spatial resolution, number of predictor variables, the complexity of the species-environment relationships, and modelling method (Moudrý et al. 2024, Santini et al. 2021, Stockwell & Peterson 2002).","This criteria can be frequently violated when modelling rare species, cryptic species, or those difficult to detect for other reasons (e.g., observable only during brief time windows; Radomski et al. 2022). Fulfilling this criteria may also be impracticable for species that have restricted geographic ranges (Santini et al. 2021). Other limitations on data availability can also lead to violation. Lastly, even generally accepted minimal sample sizes can commonly lead to violation as they reflect requirements under optimal conditions (e.g., niche stability, no dispersal limitation, no spatial position error, etc.; Moudrý et al. 2024).","It requires careful consideration of the purpose of the study (Moudrý et al. 2024)., Consider species' ecology: SDMs better predict specialist species with narrow ecological niches than generalist species with wider ecological niches (Tsoar et al. 2007) (Moudrý et al. 2024)., Consider the number of predictors investigated. As the ability to differentiate between influential and non-influential variables decreases with decreasing sample sizes (Moudrý et al. 2024)., Consider the complexity of the shape of species response curves must be taken into account as models based on small sample sizes result in less precise estimates of these shapes (Bazzichetto et al. 2023) (Moudrý et al. 2024)., Consider testing the effect of sample size (Moudrý et al. 2024; see also van van Proosdij et al. 2016)., Consider designing accurate SDMs with a well-balanced sampling of as few as 50 presences (Moudrý et al. 2024)., Subsampling; weighting; inputation (see Bowler et al. 2025)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","As Hernandez et al. (2006) point out, “[s]mall sample sizes pose challenges to any statistical analyses and result in decreased predictive potential when compared to models developed with more occurrences”. This can express itself in a few different ways. When a small sample size leads to environmental sampling bias, its consequences can be explained by violations of the criteria “Species data covers the environmental extent” (Hernandez et al. 2006). A limited sample size also constrains model complexity, that is, the model’s capacity to capture the underlying species-environmental relationships (Moudrý et al. 2024). In this case, consequences can be explained by violations of the criteria “Model complexity and structure are appropriate”.","","10, 21.1, 21.2","","10, 21.1, 21.2","12 > 10; 12 > 21.1; 12 > 21.2","Thibaud et al. 2014; Hernandez et al. 2006; Moudrý et al. 2024; Santini et al. 2021; Stockwell & Peterson 2002; Radomski et al. 2022; Tsoar et al. 2007; Bazzichetto et al. 2023; van Proosdij et al. 2016; Bowler et al. 2025"
"26","Projection","Model building","Model settings/complexity","Statistical methods and algorithms employed are appropriate","Several algorithms and approaches are now available for building SDMs. However, the appropriate choices depend primarily on the available species occurrence data and the model objective (Wiens et al. 2009, Elith & Leathwick 2009). For instance, count data require specifying an appropriate probability distribution function (e.g., Poisson, negative binomial) and an algorithm that supports it, such as generalized regressions or boosted regression trees (Guisan et al. 2017). Some methods require binary response variables (i.e., species presence-absence, or pseudoabsence), including generalized linear models (GLMs) or generalized additive models (GAMs; Wiens et al. 2009). Additionally, binary data require binomial probability distribution functions and logistic transformation (Guisan et al. 2017). Regarding the model objective, different statistical approaches are preferred when the goal is explanation, prediction and projection (Guisan et al. 2017, Elith & Leathwick 2009); although, the literature suggests that for any particular goal, there is no “best” overall model (Lawler et al. 2006).","This criteria can be easily violated when modelers use default settings in model parametrization without confirming whether they are appropriate choices for their species occurrence data (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Similarly, violation can occur through the use of an algorithm that is inappropriate for the data type or whose underlying mathematical distribution does not match the data type.","Consider ensemble models., Assess model performance; using Tru Skill Statistics (e.g. Shabani et al. 2016; Allouche et al. 2006)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption. Evaluate a set of candidate models using independent data (if available) or robust cross-validation methods to assess their fit and predictive power., Manage model complexity: Overly complex models with many parameters can overfit the data and perform poorly when extrapolating to new conditions. Balance complexity with data availability to ensure reliable predictions.","Violation of this criteria can lead to errors and uncertainty in the predictions by introducing structural biases and statistical distortions. In terms of prediction errors, consequences can be explained by violation of the related criteria “Model complexity and structure are appropriate”.","","21.1, 21.2","","21.1, 21.2","26 > 21.1; 26 > 21.2","Wiens et al. 2009; Elith & Leathwick 2009; Guisan et al. 2017; Lawler et al. 2006; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Shabani et al. 2016; Allouche et al. 2006"
"27","Projection","Model building","Model settings/complexity","Shape of the species and predictors relationships is appropriate","Related to the criteria “Model complexity and structure are appropriate”, SDMs rely on fitting a correlative relationship between the species occurrence data and predictor variables. Species responses to environmental factors are often non-linear (e.g., a bell-shaped curve describing optimal thermal tolerances, rather than a straight line; Austin 2002). Goodness-of-fit depends on properly describing the species-environmental relationships while balancing model complexity (Merow et al. 2014, Guisan et al. 2017).","This criteria is violated when modellers mischaracterize relationships between species and predictor variables (e.g., by using modelling approaches that do not handle non-linear relationships).","Transform covariates., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","When this criteria is violated, its consequences can be explained by violation of the criteria ""Model complexity and structure are appropriate"".","","21.1, 21.2","","21.1, 21.2","27 > 21.1; 27 > 21.2","Austin 2002; Merow et al. 2014; Guisan et al. 2017"
"28","Projection","Model building","Model settings/complexity","Background points or pseduo-absences are appropriate","Most SDM approaches rely on presence-only data combined with background points or pseudo-absences (Steen et al. 2024, Barbet-Massin et al. 2012). Background points correspond to points across the study area that are used to characterize the predictor variables at each site, regardless of whether species occurrence has been sampled at those points and whether the species has been detected (Araújo et al. 2019). Although the term is often used interchangeably with pseudo-absences, these correspond to sites chosen to represent absences, regardless of confirmation of true absences (Liu et al. 2019; also see Senay et al. 2013). Although many approaches exist for selecting background points and pseudo-absence points, the accuracy of SDMs depends on choosing the appropriate method given the modelling context (Steen et al. 2024, Senay et al. 2013, Barbet-Massin et al. 2012).","This criteria is violated in three main ways: if the background points are not representative of the available environment space to appropriately describe the species niche (Steen et al. 2024, Barbet-Massin et al. 2012); similarly, if pseudo-absences are either restricted to an overly tight geographic buffer around known presences or taken from an overly broad area (Barbet-Massin et al. 2012); and if the criteria “Unbiased species data” and “Biases and noise in species datasets are treated” have been violated (e.g., randomly selecting background points and/or pseudo-absences when presence data is highly biased/clustered; Phillips et al. 2009).","Assess predcitive performance; using different types of background selections (Steen et al. 2024)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","When this criteria is violated by background points that are not representative of the species environment space, its consequences can be explained by violation of the criteria “Species data covers the environmental extent”. If this criteria is violated through violation of the criteria “Biases and noise in species datasets are treated”, see criteria “Unbiased species data” for consequences. When violation happens due to pseudo-absences that are overly close to presence points, thus likely corresponding to suitable habitat, models are known to underestimate suitable habitat (Chefaoui & Lobo 2008). In contrast, when pseudo-absences are taken from an overly broad area that captures different environmental conditions than those experienced by the species, models suffer from an artificially inflated sense of confidence. By failing to learn to distinguish subtle environmental requirements, the model results in overestimation of suitable habitat (Barbet-Massin et al. 2012). These cases of prediction error apply to both prediction and projection models.","","10","10","10","28 > 10; 28 > 9 > 10","Steen et al. 2024; Barbet-Massin et al. 2012; Araújo et al. 2019; Liu et al. 2019; Senay et al. 2013; Phillips et al. 2009; Chefaoui & Lobo 2008"
"29","Projection","Model building","Reducing predictors","Predictor variables are appropriately reduced, if applicable","Predictor variable reduction is a common approach for treating collinearity and reducing model complexity to minimize overfitting (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). However, steps should be taken to ensure that variable reduction is done without compromising the model’s ability to fit nuances if informative data are discarded (even if variables might be collinear; Dormann et al. 2013), thus reducing the predictive ability of the model (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024).","This criteria is violated when modellers apply variable reduction methods without considering the ecological relevance of variables (e.g., through pre-determined cutoffs in correlation analyses; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Araújo et al. 2019).","Assess spatial autocorrelation in model residuals., Use spatial autoregressive models., Use spatial eigenvector mapping., Remove collinear variables to reduce redundancy., Reduce dimenssiionality (Zhang et al. 2023)., Orthogonal Principal Componenents (Farrell et al. 2019)., Algorithms might account for redundant variables (e.g.; Feng et al. 2019)., Select environmental variables for groups of species with similar natural histories (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024) ., Variable selection approach (Cobos et al. 2019)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","Violation of this criteria leads to violation of the related criteria “Model complexity and structure are appropriate”.","","21.1, 21.2","","21.1, 21.2","29 > 21.1; 29 > 21.2","Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Dormann et al. 2013; Araújo et al. 2019; Zhang et al. 2023; Farrell et al. 2019; Feng et al. 2019; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Cobos et al. 2019"
"32","Projection","Model assessment","Validation","Model training and validation datasets are appropriate","As Araújo et al. (2019) point out, “[a] key step in evaluating models is to compare their results against statistically independent data”. The golden standard is to use species occurrence data that are spatially or temporally independent from the training data (i.e., from separate geographic areas or data collected in different time periods; e.g., Finn et al. 2024, Hintze et al. 2021). When fully independent data is not available, training and validation datasets can be created by subsetting the data following an appropriate data partitioning method given the data structure and model objective (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Araújo et al. 2019, Le Rest et al. 2014, Araújo et al. 2005). For prediction models, although less ideal, evaluation can be also done by sub-sampling the training data when the sample size is small (e.g., Hijmans et al. 2012).","When independent data is not available, this criteria can be easily violated when creating training and validation sets since most observations are related to each other in a spatial context (Le Rest et al. 2014). In this case, the main way violation can occur is by employing data partitioning methods that rely on random splits of the data; despite being a well supported collection of methods (e.g., k-fold partitioning, bootstrapping, jack-knifing), random splits of occurrence data do not ensure statistical independence or treat biases, and therefore are still sensitive to spatial and/or temporal autocorrelation in the data (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Araújo et al. 2005).","Splitting data non-randomly (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024)., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","Violation of this criteria will compromise the ability of the validation step to detect a model that fits biased and/or autocorrelated training data (e.g., Fourcade et al. 2018, Hijmans et al. 2012; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Therefore, its consequences can be explained by violation of the criteria “Unbiased species data” and “Biases and noise in species datasets are treated”.","","","10","10","32 > 9 > 10; 32 > 22 > 9 > 10","Araújo et al. 2019; Finn et al. 2024; Hintze et al. 2021; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Rest et al. 2014; Araújo et al. 2005; Hijmans et al. 2012; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Fourcade et al. 2018"
"22","Projection","Model building","Treatments, fittings, tunning","Biases and noise in species datasets are treated","When the criteria “Unbiased species data”, “Species data covers the environmental extent”, and/or “Species data covers the geographic extent” are violated (i.e., cannot be corrected), steps should be taken to account for such biases in the model (Araújo et al. 2019). The most supported approach for when access to unbiased data is lacking, is to reduce its effects by choosing background data with the same sampling bias (Vollering et al. 2019, Syfert et al. 2013, Phillips et al. 2009; see Soley-Guardia et al. 2024). Other approaches include: accounting for spatial autocorrelation in occurrence data, incorporating a proxy of spatial bias as a covariate, filtering occurrence data to reduce clustering across geographic and/or environmental space, weighting occurrence records so that points in oversampled areas are assigned a smaller weight (Ranc et al. 2017).","This criteria is violated when treatment of bias and noise in species datasets is not appropriate or effective at addressing the issue.","Spatial thining/filtering., Background/Pseudo-absence Point Manipulation approach., Implement Integrated Species Distribution Models (ISDMs) approach that combines data from multiple sources., Applying weights to observations can account for varying sampling reliability or effort., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","When this criteria is violated, its consequences can be explained by violation of its related criteria “Unbiased species data”.","An SDM built on statistical correlations alone and lacking ecological realism may seem robust statistically but lead to misleading results (e.g., Fourcade et al. 2014). The consequences of violation for prediction errors are, however, context dependent. If the model neglects biotic constraints or positive biotic interactions, its consequences are defined by violations to the “Eltonian noise” criteria. If the model neglects anthropogenic and/or geographic constraints, its consequences are defined by violations to the “No dispersal limitation” criteria. If the model fails to account for the ability to adapt to new environments, its consequences are defined by violations to the “Genotype and phenotype stability” criteria. Also see criteria “Predictors are relevant for species response” for more information.","","10","10","22 > 9 > 10","Araújo et al. 2019; Vollering et al. 2019; Syfert et al. 2013; Phillips et al. 2009; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Ranc et al. 2017; Fourcade et al. 2014"
"23","Projection","Model building","Treatments, fittings, tunning","Collinearity in predictors is treated","SDMs assume there is no collinearity between predictors (i.e., non-independence of predictors via a linear relationship; Dormann et al. 2013).","Violation of this criteria occurs when failing to treat collinearity in predictors or when treatment is not appropriate or does not correctly address the issue (Araújo et al. 2019). However, see criteria “Predictor variables are appropriately reduced, if applicable”.","The simplest approach is to identify highly correlated variables (often using a correlation matrix or the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)) and remove one from each highly correlated pair., ""Implement dimensionality reduction techniques (PCAs Partial least squares, etc.)."", ""Algorithm solutions (regularization techniques, type of algorithm, etc.)."", Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","When SDMs are built using strongly co-linear or correlated predictors, their effects on the response variable cannot be separated, leading to severe structural instability (Araújo et al. 2019). In the case of projection models, if the relationship between these variables changes across space and/or time, models will result in erroneous results that may underestimate and/or overestimate suitable habitat (Dormann et al. 2013). In this case, its consequences for prediction error can be explained by violation of the criteria “Niche stability”.","When geographic sampling biases exist, these can translate into biased species-environment relationships due to niche truncation, and thus violate the criteria “Species data covers the environmental extent ”.","2","","2","23 > 2","Dormann et al. 2013; Araújo et al. 2019"
"20","Projection","Data quality, relevance and preparation","Predictors datasets","Non-novel conditions","Projection SDMs assume that future scenarios or transfer locations are within the range of known conditions experienced by the species in the training time and location (i.e., analogous conditions; Araújo et al. 2019, Richmond et al. 2010). For a related case that affects both prediction and projection models, see criteria “Species data covers the environmental extent”.","This criteria is commonly violated by projection models, as future times and/or transfer locations are likely to experience novel conditions. For example, when modelling invasion, violation can occur via new biotic interactions in the introduced area (Strayer et al. 2006). When modelling the effects of climate change on a species distribution, new temperature extremes and/or regimes are often predicted by climate models; Anderson 2013). Additionally, the relationships between predictor variables may change across space and/or time, which can affect the ability of the model to extrapolate (Barry and Elith 2006).","Use a clamping procedure to limit predictions in regions with novel climatic conditions., Acknowledge modelers were unable to address this assumption.","Violation of this criteria requires model extrapolation (i.e., making predictions in conditions beyond those used in model training by following response curves beyond the point of truncation), which is known to decrease model performance (Soley-Guardia et al. 2024, Feng et al. 2019; see also criteria “Extrapolation approach is appropriate”). If non-analog conditions are present in the transfer area, the assumption of niche stability is violated. Therefore, the consequences for prediction error are explained by violation of the criteria “Niche stability”.","When geographic sampling biases exist, these can translate into biased species-environment relationships due to niche truncation, and thus violate the criteria “Species data covers the environmental extent ”.","2","","2","20 > 2","Araújo et al. 2019; Richmond et al. 2010; Strayer et al. 2006; Anderson 2013; Barry & Elith 2006; Soley-Guardia et al. 2024; Feng et al. 2019"

﻿Term,Definition,Examples,References
Application category,A group of model applications sharing broad objectives and ways of using SDM outputs to inform conservation decisions. Error severity is assigned at this level in the framework.,Anthropogenic-disturbance screening belongs to the category “Threshold for restriction or precautionary management.”,This study
Core criterion,A model criterion assigned error certainty rankings and directly filtered by the framework for the selected model type.,Perfect detection is a core criterion retained for underprediction in the prediction-model case study.,This study
Criterion violation,Failure to meet a condition represented by a model criterion.,Species records cover only a narrow portion of the environmental conditions across which the model is applied.,This study
Decision threshold,"A value or rule used to translate model outputs, or quantities derived from them, into a category or action.",Locations exceeding a specified predicted-occurrence value are flagged for precautionary review.,This study
Error certainty,"The ranked likelihood that violation of a criterion will produce a particular error type for a given model type. Rankings are always, sometimes, or rarely (Table 3).","In the case study, violation of the perfect detection criterion is ranked as always leading to underprediction for prediction models.",This study
Error certainty tolerance,A user-defined selection specifying the minimum error certainty considered when identifying relevant core criteria.,Selecting sometimes retains criteria whose violation is ranked as sometimes or always producing a relevant error type.,This study
Error severity,"The ranked consequence of a particular error type for conservation outcomes within an application category. Rankings are correctness, quality, or efficiency (Table 3).",Underprediction in disturbance screening can leave important locations unprotected and is assigned a correctness consequence.,This study
Error severity tolerance,A user-defined selection specifying the minimum error severity considered when identifying relevant error types for an application.,"Selecting quality includes error types assigned quality or correctness consequences, but excludes those assigned only efficiency consequences.",This study
Error type,The direction of model error considered in the framework: underprediction or overprediction.,Underprediction; overprediction.,This study
Model application,The purpose for which SDM outputs are used to inform ecological understanding or conservation decisions.,Selecting restoration sites; directing invasive-species surveys; screening proposed developments for potential impacts on species.,Guisan et al. (2013); Srivastava et al. (2019); Meller et al. (2014)
Model assessment,"Judgement of whether a model is suitable for its intended application, informed by evaluation of its performance, assumptions, and limitations.",Judging whether a regional SDM is suitable for screening potential development impacts on a species.,Araújo et al. (2019); Soley-Guardia et al. (2024)
Model criterion,"An assumption or requirement used to evaluate an SDM, including conditions intended to avoid issues or hazards that can affect its predictions.",Species data cover the environmental extent; predictor resolution matches the response scale.,Araújo et al. (2019); Soley-Guardia et al. (2024)
Model cycle,"The iterative process of assembling and preparing data, building, evaluating, and refining a model, and generating predictions.","Compiling occurrence records, preparing environmental predictors, fitting and evaluating a model, and generating a prediction map.",Zurell et al. (2020)
Model evaluation,"Examination of model performance and plausibility using quantitative measures, qualitative evidence, or both.",Calculating performance measures using independent data and checking predicted distributions for ecological plausibility.,This study
Model type,The distinction between prediction and projection used in the framework to account for differences in the consequences of criterion violation.,Prediction; projection.,This study
Model user,"A person who uses SDM outputs to inform an ecological or conservation application, whether or not they developed the model.",A conservation planner using predicted distributions to identify candidate protected areas.,This study
Modeler,"A person who develops an SDM, including choices about data, model fitting, evaluation, and prediction.",An ecologist developing an SDM from bird surveys and environmental predictors.,This study
Overprediction,"Prediction of a quantity above its true value, or inclusion of locations that should not be included in a predicted distribution. For binary occurrence predictions, overprediction takes the form of false positives, also termed commission errors.",A model predicts a density of eight individuals per hectare where the true density is four.,"Mendes et al. (2020), Velazco et al. (2020)"
Prediction (model type),Use of fitted species–environment relationships to estimate a species’ distribution or associated quantities within the geographical region and time period represented by the model’s calibration data.,Mapping current bird density across the region represented by the calibration surveys.,Araujo et al. (2019)
Projection (model type),Transfer of fitted species–environment relationships to estimate a species’ distribution or associated quantities in another geographical region or time period.,Applying a model calibrated on current conditions to estimate suitable habitat under a future climate scenario.,Araujo et al. (2019)
Related criterion (special case),"A criterion represented as a special case of one or more core criteria, directly or through another related criterion. It is included through these relationships rather than independently assigned error certainty rankings.",A special case associated with two retained core criteria is displayed beneath each of them without being independently filtered.,This study
Species distribution model (SDM),"A model relating species occurrence or abundance to environmental variables to estimate distribution, habitat suitability, or density.",A model relating bird occurrence to forest cover and climate to map predicted occurrence.,Elith & Leathwick (2009)
Underprediction,"Prediction of a quantity below its true value, or omission of locations that should be included in a predicted distribution. For binary occurrence predictions, underprediction takes the form of false negatives, also termed omission errors.",A model predicts absence at a site where the species is present.,Auffret et al. (2024)
Use-case scenario,"The particular use of an SDM described by its application, model type, and user-defined error severity and certainty tolerances.","Disturbance screening using a prediction model, with correctness selected for severity tolerance and sometimes selected for certainty tolerance.",This study
